learning: Changing sensor offset alone isolates whether the single line loss per run is a late-anticipation failure. Controller gains are held at the best-scoring values, so a result is attributable to geometry.
notes: Iteration 3 package: the Builder's forward-offset test (y 0.05 to 0.07 m) on the iteration 0 geometry, with the iteration 0 controller unchanged so only the sensor offset varies. Chosen because iteration 0 is the best score (63.0) and iterations 1 and 2 both scored lower when several variables changed together.
rationale: The Builder's iteration 3 proposal changes one variable from the best-scoring design (iteration 0, score 63.0): the forward sensor offset moves from y=0.05 m to y=0.07 m. Iteration 0 had 1.0 line-loss events per run on the s-bend and slalom and max_error of 0.062 to 0.066 m, so the failure is a single late line loss rather than jitter. Iteration 1 (kp 4.5, kd 0.3, base_speed 1.4, 0.10 m track) and iteration 2 (wider span, 0.5 kg, 0.12 m body) both scored lower, so I do not change the controller gains or the speed. I keep the iteration 0 controller exactly (kp 3.0, ki 0, kd 0.2, base_speed 1.5, last_direction line loss, weights +1, +0.5, 0, -0.5, -1). This lets any change in score be attributed to the sensor offset. The geometry is passed through unchanged from the Builder: the five sensors sit at x = +0.03 to -0.03 at y = 0.07 m, with 12 mm footprints, 0.7 kg mass, 0.16 m body length and 0.12 m track. The sensor order matches the weights. The observation request keeps the full set of measurements so the next race can show line-loss timing, max_error and steering oscillation. Expected result: earlier bend reading, fewer line losses, and possibly a higher score. This is a prediction only; the controller is not tuned for the new offset, so a flat or lower score would mean the offset is not the limit.
